messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Just an update to my previous post. After seeing the posts related to actionButton in shinyIncubator in this discussion group, I modified my app to use that. That seems to help. The version of the small app with action buttons is in the following link:

http://glimmer.rstudio.com/rdabbler/testForm_new/

Here one has to click the actionButton to add or modify a project in the underlying table. Since the actionButton counter keeps increasing, I used another global variable that I reset each time so that data is sent to table only when I click the button again. The full code is uploaded in gist:

https://gist.github.com/4424361

I am interested in knowing if there is a better way to implement this. Also, is there a way to change the color of the action button.

Thanks,
Shankar

messages.body_plain:
Hi Vincent -

Those errors are coming up because at first, the values of input$dataset and input$columns aren't set -- there has to be a bit of back and forth between the server and the client before those values are set. It's also the reason that there are some error messages that are briefly visible in the browser.

I've modified the gist to add some checks for NULL. In the output functions, it checks if the inputs are NULL; if so, then the output functions just returns. This removes the errors at the console, as well as the errors in the browser.
runGist('4211337')

https://gist.github.com/4211337

-Winston

messages.body_plain:
Oh, strange, it should be fixed now. Thanks for pointing that out.

It looks like, as part of their revamping of the gist pages, Github has changed the way that pushing to gists works. In the past I've used this process to edit gists: clone the gist to a local repository, edit the files, commit, then push. But it looks like pushing to a gist doesn't work properly anymore -- it updates the remote repository, but the gist webpage doesn't show the new changes. I now see this when I push to a gist repo:

remote: WARN The dotcom gem environment is out-of-date or has yet to be bootstrapped.
remote:      Run script/bootstrap to remedy this situation.
remote: /data/github/current/config/basic.rb:98: gem environment not configured (RuntimeError)
remote:  from hooks/post-receive:12:in `require'
remote:  from hooks/post-receive:12

My guess is that this is the post-receive hook for updating the gist webpage. So it appears that, for the changes to show in the webpage, the gist must be edited from the web interface (which I've done for this example).

-Winston

messages.subject: Re: How to determine data loading progress in Shiny?
messages.subject_clean: How to determine data loading progress in Shiny?
messages.body_plain:
It shouldn't show transient error messages before showing the plot, in general--however it will if your reactivePlot function happens to throw an error. This is most common when using reactiveUI and the value is not available yet. You can avoid the error message by checking for the input value not being available and returning NULL from reactivePlot immediately, i.e. if (is.null(input$foo)) return(NULL);

To show progress, Shiny adds the "recalculating" CSS class to any output element that is in progress, you could add some CSS rules for that.

>

messages.body_plain:
Is it not possible in Shiny to have tabsets nested inside one another, so as to create a hierarchical structure of pages?  More generally: Is it possible in Shiny to nest any page type inside of another one?

messages.subject: R-Ring
messages.subject_clean: R-Ring
messages.body_plain:
Before I got to looking at R-Shiny (Which is lovely) I explored a lot of different tech.

One of these was clojure-ring/noir/compojure, which has analogues in other languages.

Requests to the server are in the form server:/a/b/c or similar, where a/b/c/ can be names of services, or arguments to the service.

The service is rest-ful which usually means there is no server-carried state (that matters).

This also supports XHR (XML Http Request) so JS can ask for more (or more detailed) data.

Is there any support for such a thing in R?  My d3 application is increasingly drifting away from how I understand the Shiny use-case, in the following ways:

  * a single javascript component makes request for a different record, or more detail from the current record
  * URL should reflect the current view, either using a PATH or ? or # component
  * reactives in the current sense do too much work, since they are based on push from inputs, not pull from outputs

It would be great if I could understand the problem in terms of the current shiny implementation (anyone?), but otherwise I will start looking for a ring-type solution on R.

-Alex Brown

messages.subject: Re: R-Ring
messages.subject_clean: R-Ring
messages.body_plain:
Hi Alex, thanks for the feedback!

It's early days for Shiny, we're just laying the foundation right now. You're at the ragged edge of what Shiny is capable of today, but what you're trying to do is directly in our crosshairs.

If all you want is what ring/noir/compojure provide, you should take a look at Jeffrey Horner's Rook <http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/Rook/index.html> package plus rApache <http://rapache.net/>.

> a single javascript component makes request for a different record, or more detail from the current record

This will be a central scenario for Shiny moving forward. For the current version of Shiny I didn't want to go too far down this road until we had adequate user feedback for the simpler stuff. The main challenge for Shiny, as I see it, is to see whether the reactive-programming paradigm can work at least as well as imperative programming when the lines between input and output start to blur. So far I think we have reason to be fairly optimistic :)

> URL should reflect the current view

This is out of scope for Shiny for now. We do want to enable bookmarking/sharing via URL but it's not at all clear that we'll end up with pretty URLs like the ones you're talking about, as they need to capture all the input state which might be arbitrarily complicated (nested data structures, large amounts of data, etc.).

> reactives in the current sense do too much work, since they are based on push from inputs, not pull from outputs

We're working on this right now. You can try a prototype:

install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("shiny", "rstudio", branch="jcheng/lazy-reactive-functions")

which is one easy fix (not guaranteed to be the final one though). We're also working on having non-visible outputs not do work. It's really important to us to get this right!

On Wed, Jan 2, 2013 at 8:16 PM, Alex Brown <alexb...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Before I got to looking at R-Shiny (Which is lovely) I explored a lot of different tech.
>
> One of these was clojure-ring/noir/compojure, which has analogues in other languages.
>
> Requests to the server are in the form server:/a/b/c or similar, where a/b/c/ can be names of services, or arguments to the service.
>
> The service is rest-ful which usually means there is no server-carried state (that matters).
>
> This also supports XHR (XML Http Request) so JS can ask for more (or more detailed) data.
>
> Is there any support for such a thing in R?  My d3 application is increasingly drifting away from how I understand the Shiny use-case, in the following ways:
>
>   * a single javascript component makes request for a different record, or more detail from the current record
>   * URL should reflect the current view, either using a PATH or ? or # component
>   * reactives in the current sense do too much work, since they are based on push from inputs, not pull from outputs
>
> It would be great if I could understand the problem in terms of the current shiny implementation (anyone?), but otherwise I will start looking for a ring-type solution on R.

>
> -Alex Brown
>
> --
>
>

messages.subject: Re: Initial thoughts on shiny, ggplot and d3
messages.subject_clean: Initial thoughts on shiny, ggplot and d3
messages.body_plain:
> I see 4 routes to this being a reality, with different pros and cons.
>
> 1) d3 Display backend to R.
>
> Much like R can print to pdf, svg, png, cairo, add a d3 backend.
>  Interactivity would then have to either be automatic, or retrofitted to
> metadata in grid, ggplot etc.  This would be solid and widely compatible
> with R plot types

My sense is that d3 <-> R graphics device is a poor conceptual match
and is unlikely to be that helpful (i.e. it would probably produce js
code that would not be hand editable).  I think gridSVG (http://
sjp.co.nz/projects/gridsvg/ <http://sjp.co.nz/projects/gridsvg/>) already solves the problem at this level.

> 2) Grid to d3 converter.
>
> Probably easier to write an initial version of, a function which takes a
> Grid object and sends the primitives to d3.  Likely to be a bulky data
> format, since the same data may be carried different ways (repeated grob
> descriptions, implied range in scales and plots etc).  It also would be
> more difficult to complete since grid is large and extensible.
>
> Would work with lattice and ggplot, but not base plot

I think grid <-> d3 would be a better match than graphics devices in
general, but it would be hard to map interactivity on top of grid.

> 3) Ggplot_build to d3 converter
>
> Once you have declaratively specified your plot in ggplot using geoms,
> scales, data, stats, position, facets and aesthetics, ggplot uses
> ggplot_build to internally process the data structures - and creates a new
> object with all of the work done.
>
> This would be a neat place to intercede, although my initial pass over this
> wasn't as happy as I would like; the data is not truly meant to be human
> readable, some data is implicit or spread out, and it's possible the format
> will change in the future.

Have you looked at the output from print.ggplot?  This should be
relatively straightforward to convert to json and a useful sequence of
js calls.

I think working at this level is useful, and relatively easy, but not
what I'm aiming for long term.  (So if you wanted to contribute, this
would be a great place to start)

> 4) Complete port of ggplot into d3.
>
> In this scheme, you essentially send the unprocessed ggplot object (or just
> the declaration) up to d3, and it does all the work.  That's my current
> approach, since it gets d3 native performance and style, plus lots of
> flexibility.

Yes, that's what I'm aiming for too, and I'd love to see what you have
to date.  Another really interesting consequence of this idea is that
since most of the visualisation logic is in js, it would be relatively
easy to have backends in multiple programming languages...

Hadley

Yes, I have had a look at that, and took a first pass at consuming some of it.  One challenge I encountered was that the data I need:

* aesthetic mapping
* raw data
* factor levels

are spread through the $data and $plot elements, and while most are present, it wasn't clear to me if I could reliably reconsititute them.

For example, in a bar chart the values ymin, dmax appear in the $data object.  However, they are generated by a stat, and it's not clear I can programmatically relate those back to the original named data item (they aren't in plot$mapping or plot$labels) without adding too much special knowledge in the decoder (visit the scale?).  PANEL is yet more complex; there IS NO aesthetic to map it back to.

In general this seems tractable and relatively attractive, though.

messages.subject: Re: equivalent of %in% for conditionalPanel?
messages.subject_clean: equivalent of %in% for conditionalPanel?
messages.body_plain:
I have had a lot of pleasure from underscore.js <http://underscore.js> (Thanks Joe).  Not only does it attempt to solve some of the problems you want to solve, it is also it a good way to get clues on how ordinary javascript works.

For example, map is an underscore function which iterates across a data structure, either an array or an object (there is not builtin map for objects)

In a browser debug console you can type the function name and see the internals.

> _.map
function (e, t, n) {var r=[];return p&&e.map===p?e.map(t,n):(N(e,function(e,i,s){r[r.length]=t.call(n,e,i,s)}),r);}

This is the minified version of underscore, hence the crummy short names.  Let's visit the development version <http://underscorejs.org/underscore.js> to see it in 'human':

  _.map = _.collect = function(obj, iterator, context) {
    var results = [];
    if (obj == null) return results;
    if (nativeMap && obj.map === nativeMap) return obj.map(iterator, context);
    each(obj, function(value, index, list) {
      results[results.length] = iterator.call(context, value, index, list);
    });
    return results;
  };

I wanted to see how object iteration worked, and it's delegated to 'each' which is also an underscore function

_.each= ...
   for (var key in obj) {
        if (_.has(obj, key)) {
          if (iterator.call(context, obj[key], key, obj) === breaker) return;
        }
      }
...

So it turns out it uses for (var key in obj) to iterate over an object; I've learned something new about javascript.

-Alex

messages.subject_clean: Interactive input of data
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have a question, for which the answer is probably no, but I just want to make sure :) Is there a way to do interactive data input with shiny? Now you can change single values, but I need something more: directly editing a table, ie. change the values in a data.frame which stay changed. Alternatively I would like be able to move a line in a plot, which will result in changed data.

The simple user case is prediction. Say estimate linear relationship between y and x. Then given the newdata I want to display the predictions based on it. The trick is that newdata provided is only one scenario. I would like for user of the app to change the scenarios of x to see how y changes. For that I need to interactively edit newdata. One way would be to edit the values of newdata directly, another would be to display the initial newdata on the graph and let the user change the graph. All the changes in the newdata would have to be reflected immediately in the prediction of y. This would be some kind of analytics dashboard. Is this at all possible?

Vaidotas Zemlys

These kinds of components certainly could be written with Shiny but I don't believe anyone has done so yet. With Shiny, most things are possible, it's just a question of how much JavaScript you have to write (which you can then package up so any R users can take advantage of your work).

We do have a tableInput function in the shinyIncubator package that might help, it provides a 2D table editing widget. You can install the package like so:

install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("shiny-incubator", "rstudio")

messages.subject: New isolate feature (helps with actionButton)
messages.subject_clean: New isolate feature (helps with actionButton)
messages.body_plain:
A number of you have tried to use the actionButton that's included in shiny-incubator to perform actions, and sometimes those actions needed to read from other reactive inputs. Until now, changes to those other inputs would cause the action to be re-executed, with no clean way to suppress those extra executions.

We just checked in a change to the GitHub repository that should improve things quite a bit. I'm not sure this will be our final solution to this problem, but welcome your feedback.

The change is a new function called "isolate", and it lets you execute code that reads from reactive values/functions, without having their reactivity "infect" the caller.

So a reactive data frame that only recalculates itself when an action button (with the id "recalcButton") is pressed might look like this:

mydata <- reactive(function() {
  # Don't do anything until after the first button push.
  if (input$recalcButton == 0)
    return(NULL)

  # Note that just by virtue of checking the value of input$recalcButton,
  # we're now going to get called whenever it is pushed.

  return(isolate({
    # Now do the expensive stuff
    foo <- activateInterlock(input$foo)
    bar <- connectDynotherm(input$bar)
    baz <- bringInfracellsUp(input$baz)
    c(foo=foo, bar=bar, baz=baz)
  }))
})

So mydata will automatically react to changes in recalcButton (i.e. when it is pushed) but not to changes in the inputs foo, bar, or baz.

How to install

If you'd like to try isolate out for yourself, you can conveniently install the latest build from github using these commands:

install.package("devtools")  # if necessary
devtools::install_github("shiny", "rstudio")

(Glimmer users: We generally keep Glimmer synced to the version of Shiny that's on CRAN, so isolate probably won't be available there for at least a couple of weeks. Sorry.)

messages.subject: How to run expensive code once at start-up, and then subsequently only on user request
messages.subject_clean: How to run expensive code once at start-up, and then subsequently only on user request
messages.body_plain:
I came up with a little solution to a little problem I encountered, and am sharing it in the thought that others might find it useful and save themselves a bit of time.

I have some expensive processing that I would like to be performed once at start-up, and then again if and only if the user so requests.  I tried using the new  <https://groups.google.com/forum/?fromgroups=#!topic/shiny-discuss/l8ZcauoOtuw>isolate() function that Joe introduced yesterday <https://groups.google.com/forum/?fromgroups=#!topic/shiny-discuss/l8ZcauoOtuw>. His example shows how to keep expensive code from starting up until a specified action button is pressed. The problem: I wanted the code to run exactly once before the action button was pressed, but then subsequently only if and when the action button was pressed.

Joe's example code wouldn't quite do the trick: an action button's count variable is automatically set initially to zero, so "if(input$buttonValue==0) return(NULL)" won't run my code for me at start up.  (Sidebar note/feature request: It would be nice if it were possible to create action buttons with non-zero initial values.)

The solution, like so many others, is obvious once you see it: don't use zero as the test value.

> expensiveProcess <- reactive(function() {
>   if (input$recalcButton == -1)
>     return(NULL)
>
>   return(isolate({
>       # reset value of action button to prevent further un-requested recomputation of the expensive process
>       input$recalcButton <- -1
>
>     # Now do the expensive stuff
>     foo <- activateInterlock(input$foo)
>     bar <- connectDynotherm(input$bar)
>     baz <- bringInfracellsUp(input$baz)
>     c(foo=foo, bar=bar, baz=baz)
>   }))
> })

Some readers may react by thinking, "Well, no duh."  What can I say: it took me a bit to figure it out (employing my currently flu-fogged brain), and thought this structure might be of use to some others.

Regards,

Arthur

I am still trying to get a handle on how reactive programming works. Particularly when a reactive function is linked to a tab not shown immediately in an app. The gist link below has the code example I have been working on to illustrate my confusion.

In non-reactive R functions call each other. In reactive they keep track of each other and change and updated 'when-needed'. It is the when-needed part that is less clear. If Shiny picks up the right dependencies, great. If not, for what ever reason, what is the best way to suggest the appropriate dependencies?

In my example gist, if a dataframe is changed in the data2 function the list of variable names is changed (although *not* if varnames() is reactive for some reason) and the correct data is displayed (i.e., the first column has been dropped). As far as I can see from using options(shiny.trace=TRUE) the data1 and its function are not called again to show the updated version of the data (in the Data1 tab) but rather a cached version is used.

Again, if Shiny picks up the right dependencies, great. If not what is the best way to suggest the appropriate dependencies? Also, what is the best way to visualize what reactive link are being used?

I have been stuck on this issue for some time now and could really use some help. Thanks.

messages.subject: Re: trying to understand reactivity
messages.subject_clean: trying to understand reactivity
messages.body_plain:
If you call a reactive function and then call it again without changing any of the inputs, then it uses a cached copy of the output, as you found. Shiny should always pick up the correct dependencies; if it fails to do so, then that's buggy behavior.

As for visualizing the reactive dependencies, right now there isn't an easy way to do that, sorry! One of the things we want to do in the future is develop a tool for generating visualizations for this.

-Winston

messages.subject: Re: trying to understand reactivity
messages.subject_clean: trying to understand reactivity
messages.body_plain:
Hi Vincent,

It looks like you're currently trying to get the changedata function to run and mutate input$dataset so all the other readers of input$dataset see the changed value. Instead of a function that *updates* the data, I would go with a reactive function that *wraps* the data:

mydata <- reactive(function() {
  data <- get(input$dataset)
  data[,1] <- NULL
  data
})

Now, everything else in the gist that currently calls get(input$dataset) to get the data, should instead call mydata().

In general, if you care about non-reactive side effects (such as assign(input$dataset, ...)) then you should not be using a reactive function. Instead you should be using an observer (see ?observe), or better yet, eliminate the non-reactive side effects altogether (as the above).

Reactive function is really a misnomer. We should've called them reactive expressions. If you have a reactive function "foo", then calling foo() does not mean "execute the function". Instead it means, "give me the current value of foo and let me know if it ever becomes out of date". It's possible that calling foo() will result in the actual code of the function executing right then; it's equally possible that it won't.

I have to apologize again that we don't have this better documented. Our docs up until now have been designed for people who are just getting started and for whom this level of understanding of reactivity isn't necessary. You and the other more advanced members of the Shiny community have gotten more deep into this stuff than we were really prepared for, and we recognize that we need the docs and other resources to catch up to the community.

messages.subject: conditionalPanel and actionButton
messages.subject_clean: conditionalPanel and actionButton
messages.body_plain:
I have shiny app that uses an actionButton to process data files and then the user interacts with the output (which is where the reactivity is really useful). The data processing step generally takes tens of minutes, so the user is provided with some indication that the app is running via messages in a conditional panel and via messages in the console window. It all works as intended for the first click of the actionButton (see relevant code below), but I'm not sure how to write the conditions so that the messages display properly for subsequent clicks of the actionButton.

Thanks,

Travis

actionButton("process_files", "Process Data Files"),
conditionalPanel(
        condition <- "input.process_files > 0 && !output.results",
        br(),
        p(strong("Processing data...please wait.")),
        p("Note: Progress messages are displayed in RStudio console.")
        ),
conditionalPanel(
        condition <- "output.results",
        br(),
        p(strong("Data processing is complete!"))
        )

messages.subject: Problem reproducing ggplot2 object with Shiny
messages.subject_clean: Problem reproducing ggplot2 object with Shiny
messages.body_plain:
Hello shiny enthusiasts,

I am in the midst of writing an app to showcase my R package pitchRx <http://github.com/cpsievert/pitchRx> (still in production). Here is an example of a plot (png attached) that I wish to reproduce with shiny:

library(devtools)
install_github('pitchRx', 'cpsievert')
library(pitchRx)
data(pitches, package='pitchRx')
strikeFX(pitches, geom="hex", density1=list(des="Called Strike"), layer=facet_grid(.~stand)) #Returns ggplot2 object I wish to reproduce (with shiny)

For some reason, when I use shiny to produce the same plot, I get a funny result. It seems as though the correct left-hand plot is produced, but is cut in half with the bottom half on the right-hand plot (png attached). If you would like to reproduce the error, use this: library(shiny); runGist(4440099). When prompted by your browser, scroll down to the "Plotting Geometries" section and choose "hex". Lastly, go to the "Alter Density(ies)" section and select "des" as the first variable of interest.

It's worth noting that this issue doesn't occur for a "classic" 2D density. It seems to only happen when strikeFX plots the difference of two different 2D density estimates.

Thanks in advance,

-Carson

Carson Sievert
Graduate Student
3414 Snedecor Hall
Iowa State University

So let's make sure I understand you right.

1) The actual underlying data never changes.
2) Sometimes you want to add residuals or whatever.
3) Probably you don't want to calculate the residuals when they won't need to be displayed.
4) The residuals are expensive to calculate so once you calculate them, you'd like to keep them around and reuse them (unless something changes about the underlying data changes, if assumption #1 is incorrect; then they need to be recalculated when needed).

> So let's make sure I understand you right.

> > >   data[,1] <- NULL

messages.body_plain:
I have been mulling option 4 - re-implementing ggplot in d3, and I have come up with a few questions that I haven't yet worked out how to answer:

Should 'g2plot.js' be aimed at R users, or at d3/js users (or both)?  It might be usable for both either way, but we could think on the following issues:

  * Should we expect all data prep be done in R, or provide facilities to do data prep in JS? (think reshape, extending stat_* to be more complete, etc)
  * Should the input data be general, which is to say suitable for generating multiple plots, or should it be targeted at one plot style with a specific X and Y etc?
    This is related to the first point, since while the input data may be pre-processed in R, ggplot currently also expects you to walk some of the last 'half mile' using R, and that half mile differs depending upon the expected output.  Think re-ordering factor levels, adding annotations such as labels and lines for averages (and calculating the averages) etc.
  * Is the primary command UI an R facility or a JS facility?  This has a couple of issues - if we are aiming at R users, then familiarity with R conventions is a plus, either in the JS or R interface.  We might expect to provide JS proxies for R objects such as lists (ordered hashmaps) and data frames (column major typed 2d arrays).  If we are aiming at JS users, then the converse applies, and it may be a disadvantage to require use of proxies.
  * Should the JS be assembled by R, or be a client-side library.  The first option may be better in performance and more amenable to hacking once built.  The second option is more useful but may be opaque and difficult for users to augment with their own custom fun stuff.  This is related to the idea -
  * should the solution be (primarily) powerful with a clean R/JS command interface, or simple with a clean JS code structure (like d3, that's amenable to easy customisation)?  These things keep me awake at night :-)
  * Clearly it's cheaper to target one user base than both.

We also might consider if rebuilding ggplot-like facilities allows a re-think of some basics.  I'm sure everyone has some 'if-only' ideas, but I'd be pleased to see some of the following:

  * demotion of facets to an extension of aesthetics with special scale rules.  Ordinal (factor) aesthetics may be mapped in many ways to the plot - as a x,y,wrap,page! facet, as a group, as a nested x-axis, as a stacked y axis etc etc etc.  This is currently non-orthogonal in ggplot, and needs love.
  * expansion of stat_ to cover common cases such as adding a y-mean per group, or a floating label.  This may be particularly important for JS users, (or not) depending upon if they have the skills to do the client side data prep, and if the g2plot implementation is transparent enough to allow addition.
  * less controversial is a mechanism to combine aesthetics to express a large-valued dataset - extension of e.g. 'profession' into the cross product of colors, stripes, outlines etc.

A related but complex topic is that data.table - and CSVs are poor structural representations of real data (for all that they might be clean and performant).  This impacts a few things:

  1) the structure for the (efficient) transmission of data
  2) how to relate csv structured data to the underlying (more complex) data model.  Imagine expressing the columns of a csv as the terms of a GLM (or more!)- with all the operators in use - clustering, link functions, error models.  I may be talking out of my posterior here, but that's how i think actual data IS.  are the terms of an AES also the terms of a GLM?
  3) conversion of arbitrary formats to the row-major record oriented structure currently favoured by the d3 implementation.  (I'd like to work out how to do better in my d3 - and capture context from tree parents in nodes).

Some of the problems above suggest to me that there are two projects here:

 1) create a JS data (transmission, import and) manipulation library to solve some of the above
 2) build a grammar-of-graphics interface to d3 that meets at least some of the above.

Okay, that's enough from me; what are your thoughts on this?

-Alex

Until now, changes to those other inputs would cause the action to be re-executed, with no clean way to suppress those extra executions.
>
> We just checked in a change to the GitHub repository that should improve things quite a bit. I'm not sure this will be our final solution to this problem, but welcome your feedback.
>
> The change is a new function called "isolate", and it lets you execute code that reads from reactive values/functions, without having their reactivity "infect" the caller.
>
> So a reactive data frame that only recalculates itself when an action button (with the id "recalcButton") is pressed might look like this:
>
> mydata <- reactive(function() {
>   # Don't do anything until after the first button push.
>   if (input$recalcButton == 0)
>     return(NULL)
>
>   # Note that just by virtue of checking the value of input$recalcButton,
>   # we're now going to get called whenever it is pushed.
>
>   return(isolate({
>     # Now do the expensive stuff
>     foo <- activateInterlock(input$foo)
>     bar <- connectDynotherm(input$bar)
>     baz <- bringInfracellsUp(input$baz)
>     c(foo=foo, bar=bar, baz=baz)
>   }))
> })
>
> So mydata will automatically react to changes in recalcButton (i.e. when it is pushed) but not to changes in the inputs foo, bar, or baz.
>
> How to install
>
> If you'd like to try isolate out for yourself, you can conveniently install the latest build from github using these commands:
>
> install.package("devtools")  # if necessary
> devtools::install_github("shiny", "rstudio")
>
> (Glimmer users: We generally keep Glimmer synced to the version of Shiny that's on CRAN, so isolate probably won't be available there for at least a couple of weeks. Sorry.)

messages.body_plain:
OK, interesting.

The input controls don't currently support that. Fortunately the HTML generating functions return well-structured lists of tags that are easy to munge. For example:

disable <- function(x) {
  if (inherits(x, 'shiny.tag')) {
    if (x$name %in% c('input', 'select'))
      x$attribs$disabled <- 'disabled'
    x$children <- disable(x$children)
  }
  else if (is.list(x) && length(x) > 0) {
    for (i in 1:length(x))
      x[[i]] <- disable(x[[i]])
  }
  x
}

So if you include this function definition at the top of ui.R then you could do e.g.:

sidebarPanel(
  disable(selectInput(...)),
  disable(radioButtons(...))
)

or whatever.

messages.body_plain:
Waaaaait a minute. Here's the source code for reactiveTable:

function (func, ...)
{
    reactive(function() {
        classNames <- getOption("shiny.table.class", "data table table-bordered table-condensed")
        data <- func()
        if (is.null(data) || is.na <http://is.na>(data))
            return("")
        return(paste(capture.output(print(xtable(data, ...),
            type = "html", html.table.attributes = paste("class=\"",
                htmlEscape(classNames, TRUE), "\"", sep = ""),
            ...)), collapse = "\n"))
    })
}

The problem is in bold. is.na <http://is.na> works "element-wise" so it returns a dataframe filled with TRUE/FALSE; when this is then OR'd with is.null(data) it is silently converted to TRUE.

messages.subject: Using knit2html (with brew) output in shiny
messages.subject_clean: Using knit2html (with brew) output in shiny
messages.body_plain:
Well, as is standard operating procedure around here, I'm getting vague direction on my TeachingLab demo. I've now updated it to contain the functionality of what our users here at Vanderbilt might use.

Again, here's the link to TeachingLab running on glimmer:

http://glimmer.rstudio.com/jeffreyhorner/TeachingLab/

and github:

https://github.com/jeffreyhorner/TeachingLab

The intention is to use an Rmd file to define either a portion of or all of the shiny application interface. This gives you the niceties of both knitr/markdown plus the convenience of shiny outputs:

1. Markdown markup for headings, etc.
2. Mathjax support
3. Formatted R code with syntax highlighting
4. Shiny outputs like sliders, animation, plot outputs, etc.

The above example defines a portion of it by tying teaching.Rmd <https://github.com/jeffreyhorner/TeachingLab/blob/master/teaching.Rmd> to a tab, but you could definitely do something like Yihui does in his knitr-shiny app <https://github.com/yihui/knitr/blob/master/inst/shiny/ui.R> using bootstrapPage rather than what I do with pageWithSideBar <https://github.com/jeffreyhorner/TeachingLab/blob/master/ui.R> and my customHeaderPanel <https://github.com/jeffreyhorner/TeachingLab/blob/master/shinyExtras.R#L10>.

The only hitch (and maybe a hack) is that I now brew the Rmd document before handing it off to knit2html so that I can execute R commands inline to produce the shiny HTML output. Maybe I'm missing something with knitr, because I didn't see a way of doing this solely with knitr?

What do you think?

Jeff

messages.subject: Re: trying to understand reactivity
messages.subject_clean: trying to understand reactivity
messages.body_plain:
OK I finally understood what you were trying to do with respect to modifying the dataset. I just sent you a pull request: https://github.com/mostly-harmless/damshiny/pull/1

The key here is that when you modify a value that is depended on by other reactive functions (in this case, the dataset) you need to make sure that both reads and writes happen in a way that the reactive system can be aware that something has happened. Regular gets/assign/<- do not meet those criteria.

On master, we've introduced a new feature called reactive values. You use the reactiveValue function to create them. They behave sort of like when you read input$foo; whenever input$foo changes in the future, any reactive functions will know they are out of date. In the same way, when you read a reactive value, when that reactive value changes in the future you'll be notified. However, the difference is that you can write reactive values as well. This is what you were asking for further back in this(?) thread but I didn't think it's what you actually needed at the time.

Create reactive values like this:

  foo <- reactiveValue(100) # initial value of 100

Read them like this:

  value(foo)

Write them like this:

  value(foo) <- 200

In your particular case, you have multiple datasets that you want to reference dynamically (i.e. not hard coding the name), so I created an environment to hold them. Another solution in the future will be to use a Values object, which looks sort of like an environment (or dictionary/hashtable in other languages) but is reactive-aware:

datasets <- shiny:::Values$new()
datasets$set("mtcars", mtcars)
isolate({
  print(datasets$get("mtcars"))
})

Values' set/get operations are reactive-aware, and they are implemented slightly more efficiently than what I did in your pull request. Also it has the advantage that if you call Values$get with a name that doesn't exist in the list yet, then if it's later added, you'll be notified (and vice versa--if you get a value that is later removed, you will also be notified).

This is probably a lot to digest already--I've leave it there.

messages.body_plain:
Thanks to all for commenting on this. I was trying to do a similar (but perhaps simpler) thing to indicate that work is happening in the background while the user waits: display an animated gif. I used the conditionalPanel() function in ui.R to show the image when a somewhat lengthy simulation is running:

conditionalPanel(condition="$('html').hasClass('shiny-busy')", img(src="loading.gif")),

The only drawback is that it does not show on initial page load (there is probably another condition that I could use for this). Anyhow, this might be helpful for others trying to indicate progress without using additional JavaScript.

Do this as soon as you set the value, there's no need to wait until submit is pressed.

On Friday, 4 January 2013 13:28:20 UTC-8, Joe Cheng [RStudio] wrote:

> A number of you have tried to use the actionButton that's included in shiny-incubator to perform actions, and sometimes those actions needed to read from other reactive inputs. Until now, changes to those other inputs would cause the action to be re-executed, with no clean way to suppress those extra executions.
>
> We just checked in a change to the GitHub repository that should improve things quite a bit. I'm not sure this will be our final solution to this problem, but welcome your feedback.
>
> The change is a new function called "isolate", and it lets you execute code that reads from reactive values/functions, without having their reactivity "infect" the caller.
>
> So a reactive data frame that only recalculates itself when an action button (with the id "recalcButton") is pressed might look like this:
>
> mydata <- reactive(function() {
>   # Don't do anything until after the first button push.
>   if (input$recalcButton == 0)
>     return(NULL)
>
>   # Note that just by virtue of checking the value of input$recalcButton,
>   # we're now going to get called whenever it is pushed.
>
>   return(isolate({
>     # Now do the expensive stuff
>     foo <- activateInterlock(input$foo)
>     bar <- connectDynotherm(input$bar)
>     baz <- bringInfracellsUp(input$baz)
>     c(foo=foo, bar=bar, baz=baz)
>   }))
> })
>
> So mydata will automatically react to changes in recalcButton (i.e. when it is pushed) but not to changes in the inputs foo, bar, or baz.
>
> How to install
>
> If you'd like to try isolate out for yourself, you can conveniently install the latest build from github using these commands:
>
> install.package("devtools")  # if necessary
> devtools::install_github("shiny", "rstudio")
>
> (Glimmer users: We generally keep Glimmer synced to the version of Shiny that's on CRAN, so isolate probably won't be available there for at least a couple of weeks. Sorry.)

Values has been there since day 1, it's just not exported. So you can use it today by saying shiny:::Values$new() instead of just Values$new(). The downside of this is that we could rename it (and probably will, to something more descriptive like ReactiveValues) at any time since it's not part of the public API.

To set something into an environment, use assign(name, value, pos=datasetEnv). So in this case,
  assign(file, reactiveValue(read.csv(...)), pos=datasetEnv)

Then read it with
  value(get(file, pos=datasetEnv))

and modify it with
  value(get(file, pos=datasetEnv)) <- newvalues

messages.subject: Re: New isolate feature (helps with actionButton)
messages.subject_clean: New isolate feature (helps with actionButton)
messages.body_plain:
Joe's right, it looks like it is a bug with devtools being too strict about version checking for Rtools. One workaround, if you're using R 2.15.2, is to install Rtools215.exe from the Rtools page (even though the page says that you should install Rtools216.exe).
  http://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/

After you install Rtools215.exe, you should be able to run devtools::install_github() without errors.

-Winston

On Wed, Jan 9, 2013 at 2:50 PM, Andrew Clark <scott.r...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Tx Once I twigged That I needed to drop down to the x64 subfolder it loaded
> So is that all i need? I remember reading something about the actionButton being in shiny-incubator and I had the
> same problem using devtools with that command
> devtools::install_github('shiny-incubator' , "rstudio")
>
>
> On Friday, 4 January 2013 13:28:20 UTC-8, Joe Cheng [RStudio] wrote:
> > A number of you have tried to use the actionButton that's included in shiny-incubator to perform actions, and sometimes those actions needed to read from other reactive inputs. Until now, changes to those other inputs would cause the action to be re-executed, with no clean way to suppress those extra executions.
> >
> > We just checked in a change to the GitHub repository that should improve things quite a bit. I'm not sure this will be our final solution to this problem, but welcome your feedback.
> >
> > The change is a new function called "isolate", and it lets you execute code that reads from reactive values/functions, without having their reactivity "infect" the caller.
> >
> > So a reactive data frame that only recalculates itself when an action button (with the id "recalcButton") is pressed might look like this:
> >
> > mydata <- reactive(function() {
> >   # Don't do anything until after the first button push.
> >   if (input$recalcButton == 0)
> >     return(NULL)
> >
> >   # Note that just by virtue of checking the value of input$recalcButton,
> >   # we're now going to get called whenever it is pushed.
> >
> >   return(isolate({
> >     # Now do the expensive stuff
> >     foo <- activateInterlock(input$foo)
> >     bar <- connectDynotherm(input$bar)
> >     baz <- bringInfracellsUp(input$baz)
> >     c(foo=foo, bar=bar, baz=baz)
> >   }))
> > })
> >
> > So mydata will automatically react to changes in recalcButton (i.e. when it is pushed) but not to changes in the inputs foo, bar, or baz.
> >
> > How to install
> >
> > If you'd like to try isolate out for yourself, you can conveniently install the latest build from github using these commands:
> >
> > install.package("devtools")  # if necessary
> > devtools::install_github("shiny", "rstudio")
> >
> > (Glimmer users: We generally keep Glimmer synced to the version of Shiny that's on CRAN, so isolate probably won't be available there for at least a couple of weeks. Sorry.)
>

> --
>
>

messages.body_plain:
I was able to get something working on a private Shiny Server instance (as RGL has some dependencies which aren't available on Glimmer). You can take a look here:
https://www.trestletechnology.net/2013/01/visualize-color-palettes-in-interactive-3d-grid-shiny-rgl/

The source is available on Github if you want to play around with it: https://github.com/trestletech/shiny-sandbox/tree/master/rgl

Enjoy!
Jeff

On Wednesday, December 5, 2012 10:52:00 AM UTC-6, Joe Cheng [RStudio] wrote:
> Shiny has an htmlOutput widget that can be inserted into your Shiny app and receive arbitrary HTML. In theory you could take the webgl HTML that is outputted by rgl, and assign it in a reactive function to the output HTML:
>
> output$webglPlot <- reactive(function() {
>   // webgl generating code here, return an HTML string
> })
>
> Some things you'll have to deal with:
> By default, rgl's webgl mode outputs an entire HTML page including head and body tags, which is not quite what you want. You'll have to provide a template argument to writeWebGL, the path of a file whose entire contents are below.
> writeWebGL writes its output to a file, not a string, so you'll have to create a temp file and read in the contents. Don't forget to delete the temp file before leaving the function.
> writeWebGL takes a prefix for disambiguating different scenes on the same page. You might want to generate a random prefix for each scene that you generate.
>
> Even with all this I'm not sure if it will work, but it sure seems worth a shot. There's no inherent reason why WebGL shouldn't work with Shiny, so I'm sure that if nothing else some tweaking to rgl would make it possible. If you figure out how to get it going it would be amazing to have a reactiveWebGL function that wraps up the call to writeWebGL for you--we can help you with that if you need.
>
>
> template.html:
>
> %WebGL%
> <script>setTimeout(function() { webGLStart(); }, 100);</script>
>
>

It would be really nice if one could easily combine these two approaches to vary e.g. parameters controlling the plots. Would anyone have any suggestions for how to do this?

Until now, changes to those other inputs would cause the action to be re-executed, with no clean way to suppress those extra executions.
> > >
> > > We just checked in a change to the GitHub repository that should improve things quite a bit. I'm not sure this will be our final solution to this problem, but welcome your feedback.
> > >
> > > The change is a new function called "isolate", and it lets you execute code that reads from reactive values/functions, without having their reactivity "infect" the caller.
> > >
> > > So a reactive data frame that only recalculates itself when an action button (with the id "recalcButton") is pressed might look like this:

> > >   # we're now going to get called whenever it is pushed.
> > >
> > >   return(isolate({
> > >     # Now do the expensive stuff
> > >     foo <- activateInterlock(input$foo)
> > >     bar <- connectDynotherm(input$bar)
> > >     baz <- bringInfracellsUp(input$baz)
> > >     c(foo=foo, bar=bar, baz=baz)
> > >   }))
> > > })
> > >

> > > How to install

> > > install.package("devtools")  # if necessary
> > > devtools::install_github("shiny", "rstudio")

messages.subject: Re: ggplot not picking up variable
messages.subject_clean: ggplot not picking up variable
messages.body_plain:
Hi Andrew -

(I'm assuming that you want to use `stGame` where you've put `endGame` in your code.)
This is due to a bug in ggplot2 where it evaluates the call to aes() in the global environment, instead of the calling environment, which is what you'd normally expect. Here's the bug in the tracker:
  https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/issues/743

A couple workarounds.
- In the call to ggplot(), specify the environment:
    ggplot(..., environment = environment())

- In the geom_vline(), don't put the xintercept in aes() -- just get rid of the aes() completely. (geom_vline and geom_hline are a special cases of how they use aes.)

-Winston

> > Shiny has an htmlOutput widget that can be inserted into your Shiny app and receive arbitrary HTML. In theory you could take the webgl HTML that is outputted by rgl, and assign it in a reactive function to the output HTML:
> >
> > output$webglPlot <- reactive(function() {
> >   // webgl generating code here, return an HTML string
> > })
> >
> > Some things you'll have to deal with:
> > By default, rgl's webgl mode outputs an entire HTML page including head and body tags, which is not quite what you want. You'll have to provide a template argument to writeWebGL, the path of a file whose entire contents are below.
> > writeWebGL writes its output to a file, not a string, so you'll have to create a temp file and read in the contents. Don't forget to delete the temp file before leaving the function.
> > writeWebGL takes a prefix for disambiguating different scenes on the same page. You might want to generate a random prefix for each scene that you generate.
> >
> > Even with all this I'm not sure if it will work, but it sure seems worth a shot. There's no inherent reason why WebGL shouldn't work with Shiny, so I'm sure that if nothing else some tweaking to rgl would make it possible. messages.body_plain:
No it's not. I didn't notice that line in Arthur's code snippet. "input$recalcButton <- -1" is not necessary and in fact does nothing.

I don't know why you would need to ever reset the actionButton value.

If you want it to happen on startup and also on every button click:

reactive(function() {
  input$recalcButton
  isolate({
    # do expensive stuff here and return the result
  })
})

If you want it NOT to happen on startup, but only on button click:

reactive(function() {
  if (input$recalcButton == 0)
    return()

  isolate({
    # do expensive stuff here and return the result
  })
})

messages.subject: Wishlist suggestions
messages.subject_clean: Wishlist suggestions
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

First, let me just say that Shiny is amazing! I think it will be a real game changer in both teaching and reproducible research.

I built my own Shiny app in just a few hours:
http://glimmer.rstudio.com/smjenness/SIR/

Code at:
https://github.com/smjenness/Shiny/tree/master/SIR

I have a couple "wishlist" items for future development. I realize some of these may be currently modified through the tags functions, but I think many would find these tasks easier with function arguments.
1. a p(...) text field able to be placed under the headerPanel(...) in pageWithSidebar(...) pages. I would like to be able to move some of the text in my "About" tab to under the main page headerPanel.
2. dimension arguments (height, width) for the size of all input functions for the ui.R file, similar to those available for plotOutput(...). For example, in my app above, I would like to set the the width of the sliderInput for the linewidth function in the mainPanel, such that it would not span the entire width of the mainPanel. This would take the form, sliderInput(..., width=200px).
3. relatedly, some of the input functions in the mainPanel get clipped, whereas there is more padding in the sidebarPanel. For example, slide my line width slide all the way to the left. Is there a padding argument that could be added to the sidebarPanel function?

Finally, I would love some sort of common repository of user examples, sort of like yihui's knitr showcase (http://yihui.name/knitr/demo/showcase/), since I learned everything based on the tutorial examples and digging through people's posts on this board.

Thank you!
Samuel Jenness
Department of Epidemiology
University of Washington

Can you describe "side-effects that are not wanted"? If you change input$addoutput to an actionButton the following should give you exactly what you describe:

if (input$addoutput == 0)
  return()

isolate({

  var.name <http://var.name> <- "residuals"
  changedata(result$residuals, var.name <http://var.name>)

})

Oh, unless the problem is that changedata can take a long time and the user can click the button multiple times while they're waiting?? I could see that being a difference.

messages.body_plain:
I just did a little experiment... It looks like this is a quirk of read.csv() -- it only gives this warning when there are 5 or fewer lines in the data file (counting the header). For example, this gives the warning:

Test,Type,Desc,Start.Date,Last.Date
t1,M,Test 1,2012-12-12,2013-01-10
t2,P,Test 2,2012-12-12,2013-01-10
t3,P,Test 3,2012-12-12,2013-01-10
t4,P,Test 4,2012-12-12,2013-01-10

But this does not:
Test,Type,Desc,Start.Date,Last.Date
t1,M,Test 1,2012-12-12,2013-01-10
t2,P,Test 2,2012-12-12,2013-01-10
t3,P,Test 3,2012-12-12,2013-01-10

messages.body_plain:
If you attempt to read a reactive value from a non-reactive context, you will get that error. (Writes are fine though, you can do that anywhere.)

Let me unpack the previous statement.

A "reactive context" means there is a reactive function or an output like reactivePrint that is currently executing. When you read a reactive value (whether this new reactiveValue style or the traditional input$foo variety) you are really saying two things:

1) I want to know the current value of this thing.
2) When the value of this thing changes in the future, let me know that I may need to re-execute (we call this "invalidation" internally).

If you just execute some normal code, say in global.R, and read a reactive value, Shiny knows how to give you #1 but not #2. You're not executing in the scope of a reactive function, so when you say "let me know to re-execute" there's no "me" in existence.

If you're programming in the reactive style, then this is probably a bug anyway. That's why Shiny raises an error, to alert you of that possibility.

Once you have wrapped the data variables in value() (it doesn't need to be all the variables, just the ones that need the reactivity) if it still doesn't work, update the gist and we can take a detailed look.

We're definitely well aware of the documentation gap especially for conceptual stuff like this. It's a big priority for us to get caught up.

messages.body_plain:
I forked it here:
https://gist.github.com/4533075

There were a couple of issues but overall you were very very close. The main thing was when indexing into a dataset that is in a reactive value, you were doing:

value(data[,1])

instead should be:

value(data)[,1]

Also, in ui.R there was a condition that depended on a server-side value, and a "last updated" timestamp that also depended on a server-side value. Since these values can change over time, they need to be set on the server using output$foo and then access in ui.R using "output.foo" for the conditional case, and "htmlOutput" and similar functions for the latter case.

Finally, I fixed the error message by wrapping an "isolate" call around the value() calls in global.R. The "isolate" function is basically you telling Shiny that you only care about the current values of the reactive stuff, and to throw away any notifications. I made this an explicit function call rather than the default behavior when you're not running in a reactive context, so that you would be forced to really consider whether this is what you want. In this case, the other way to go would have been to introduce new variables to hold the non-reactive values before assigning them to the reactive values, and reusing them:

current.time <- Sys.time()
current.ab.info <http://current.ab.info> <- get.ab.info <http://get.ab.info>()
data.updated <- reactiveValue(current.time)  # when this code fist ran and the files grabbed
ab.info <http://ab.info> <- reactiveValue(current.ab.info <http://current.ab.info>)
exp.results <- reactiveValue(get.exp.results())

# what is the max data from Last.Date in the test info file? An updated file friom the warehouse would have yesterdays date

data.age <- reactiveValue(as.integer(as.Date(current.time) - as.Date(max(current.ab.info <http://current.ab.info>$Last.Date))))

messages.subject: Re: a non-reactive button with a resetable value
messages.subject_clean: a non-reactive button with a resetable value
messages.body_plain:
Hi Vincent,

I spent most of today looking at your code, it turned out to be extremely interesting because there is a circular dependency in there. main.regression both reads and writes the dataset.

I made a fix that puts the button-handling code in a much more sensible place, and sent you a pull request, BUT it looks like I was using a version of your code that was two commits back. I couldn't understand the last two commits with a quick look and don't have more time today to look at it. But I wanted to explain to you what is different about my commit, so you can figure out the right thing to do to your current code.

The core issue was that main.regression contained the button-handling code. That means it is handling two completely distinct tasks: calculating the regression, and responding to the button clicks. These are not only two distinct tasks, but they are also distinct in nature: the former task has no side effects, its return value is depended upon by other reactive stuff, and you can trust the reactive system to let it run whenever; the latter task is all side effect (updating the data), nothing depends on it directly, and it MUST only execute when the button is clicked.

To me that means these are screaming to be two separate entities. Calculating the regression is a reactive function, and handling the button click is an observer (using the actionButton/isolate pattern to make sure it only runs on click).

Once I extracted the button handling code and put it in its own observer, everything seemed to work.

On Tuesday, January 15, 2013 4:43:43 PM UTC-8, Joe Cheng [RStudio] wrote:
> Hi Vincent,
>
> I spent most of today looking at your code, it turned out to be extremely interesting because there is a circular dependency in there. main.regression both reads and writes the dataset.
>
> I made a fix that puts the button-handling code in a much more sensible place, and sent you a pull request, BUT it looks like I was using a version of your code that was two commits back. I couldn't understand the last two commits with a quick look and don't have more time today to look at it. But I wanted to explain to you what is different about my commit, so you can figure out the right thing to do to your current code.
>
> The core issue was that main.regression contained the button-handling code. That means it is handling two completely distinct tasks: calculating the regression, and responding to the button clicks. These are not only two distinct tasks, but they are also distinct in nature: the former task has no side effects, its return value is depended upon by other reactive stuff, and you can trust the reactive system to let it run whenever; the latter task is all side effect (updating the data), nothing depends on it directly, and it MUST only execute when the button is clicked.
>
> To me that means these are screaming to be two separate entities. Calculating the regression is a reactive function, and handling the button click is an observer (using the actionButton/isolate pattern to make sure it only runs on click).
>
> Once I extracted the button handling code and put it in its own observer, everything seemed to work.

On Wednesday, January 16, 2013 10:59:15 AM UTC-8, Vincent wrote:
> Glad I could be of assistance :)
>
> On Wednesday, January 16, 2013 9:45:30 AM UTC-8, Joe Cheng [RStudio] wrote:
> > No no, it was great. We were wondering whether circular dependencies worked or not. It turns out it works fine on the released version of Shiny, but did not on our upcoming version--so damshiny helped us find and fix a pretty gnarly bug!
> >
> > So, thank you!
> >
> >
> > On Wed, Jan 16, 2013 at 1:54 AM, Vincent <mostly.ha...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > Wow. Sorry to cause so much trouble :) The latest commits had a similar idea of separating the regression and the button handling code. I'll change this to use an observer.
> > >
> > > Thanks Joe!
> > >
> > > On Tuesday, January 15, 2013 4:43:43 PM UTC-8, Joe Cheng [RStudio] wrote:
> > > > Hi Vincent,
> > > >
> > > > I spent most of today looking at your code, it turned out to be extremely interesting because there is a circular dependency in there. main.regression both reads and writes the dataset.
> > > >
> > > > I made a fix that puts the button-handling code in a much more sensible place, and sent you a pull request, BUT it looks like I was using a version of your code that was two commits back. I couldn't understand the last two commits with a quick look and don't have more time today to look at it. But I wanted to explain to you what is different about my commit, so you can figure out the right thing to do to your current code.
> > > >
> > > > The core issue was that main.regression contained the button-handling code. That means it is handling two completely distinct tasks: calculating the regression, and responding to the button clicks. These are not only two distinct tasks, but they are also distinct in nature: the former task has no side effects, its return value is depended upon by other reactive stuff, and you can trust the reactive system to let it run whenever; the latter task is all side effect (updating the data), nothing depends on it directly, and it MUST only execute when the button is clicked.
> > > >
> > > > To me that means these are screaming to be two separate entities. Calculating the regression is a reactive function, and handling the button click is an observer (using the actionButton/isolate pattern to make sure it only runs on click).
> > > >
> > > > Once I extracted the button handling code and put it in its own observer, everything seemed to work.
> > > >
> > > >

I was able to get select2 working. Very nice although the font is smaller than I would like. Haven't figured out how to change that yet.

To make this work get the files from https://github.com/ivaynberg/select2 and put them in www/js/

Then put the following in a file in www/js/myselect2.js where tool is your shiny selectInput

<link href="js/select2.css" rel="stylesheet"/>
<script src="js/select2.js"></script>
<script>
    $(document).ready(function() { $("#tool").select2({ width: 'resolve' }); });
</script>

Then in ui.R

includeHTML("www/js/myselect2.js"),
selectInput(inputId = "tool", label = "Tool:", choices = toolChoices, selected = 'Data view')

messages.body_plain:
Firstly shiny is fantastic (thanks), but of course we always want it to do more !

I don't know javascript so apologies if I've missed something obvious.

I want to populate a selectInput() choice box with results from server, and have been trying for a day with no success. I've created a toy example in which you'll see I abandoned an initially logical approach and tried brute force with various failed trials commented out.

Any hints appreciated.
Thanks,
Andy

UI.r
library(shiny)

# Define UI
shinyUI(pageWithSidebar(

  # Application title
  h5("to test populating UI selectInput from server result, Andy South, 17/01/2013"),

  # Sidebar with controls
  sidebarPanel(

    sliderInput("numSpSelected", "Top X species",
                min = 1, max = 6, value = 2, step= 1)

    ,selectInput("variable", "Choose a species : (I want the number of species to be defined by the slider above)"
                 #,choices = output.getSelectedSpecies) #fails: object 'output.getSelectedSpecies' not found
                 #,choices = getSelectedSpecies) #fails: object 'getSelectedSpecies' not found
                 ,choices = "getSelectedSpecies") #populates box with the text "getSelectedSpecies"
                 #,choices = output$getSelectedSpecies) #fails: object 'output' not found
                 #,choices = output.speciesSubset)# fails:
                 #,choices = output.speciesSubset())# fails:could not find function "output.speciesSubset"

    #this used to get a list of selected species into the UI, now seems not to
    #,uiOutput("getSelectedSpecies")

    #this doesn't seem to do anything
    #,conditionalPanel( condition = "getSelectedSpecies"
    ,conditionalPanel( condition = TRUE
      ,selectInput("variable", "Choose a species :"
                  , choices = "getSelectedSpecies")
      ) #end of conditionalPanel

  ),

  ## MAIN PANEL ##
  mainPanel(
    h4("full species list")
    ,textOutput("caption")
  ) # end of mainPanel

)) #end of ui.R

server.R
library(shiny)

dFSpecies <- data.frame(Name=c("ginkgo","rowan","oak","ash","beech","maple"))

# Define server logic
shinyServer(function(input, output) {

  #to provide a list of selected species based on input parameters
  #doesn't quite seem to work, may be because shiny doesn't allow
  #return of a dataframe to the UI
  #can return a tagList
  getSelectedSpecies <- reactiveUI(function() {

    return(list(dFSpecies$Name[c(1:input$numSpSelected)]))

  }) #end of getSelectedSpecies

  output$speciesSubset <- reactiveUI(function() {
    getSelectedSpecies()
  })

  # return the full list
  output$caption <- reactiveText(function() {
    as.character(dFSpecies$Name)
  })

}) # end of shinyServer()

#end of server.R

messages.subject: Re: Offline Installation-Package for Shiny-Server
messages.subject_clean: Offline Installation-Package for Shiny-Server
messages.body_plain:
I just added a script to the GitHub repository to let you build an offline installer for the shiny-server package itself. You will still have to install Node.js, R, and the Shiny R package (along with its dependencies) though.

For the Shiny R package, if you have either an Internet-connected server or a virtual machine that has the same OS version installed (including 32 vs. 64 bit) then you could install the Shiny package and copy the entire site library (on Ubuntu, for example, it's /usr/local/lib/R/site-library).

For the Shiny Server package, do this on an Internet-connected machine with git and Node.js installed:

git clone https://github.com/rstudio/shiny-server
cd shiny-server
node tools/bundle-offline-installer.js

That will generate a file like "shiny-server-0.2.2.tgz" in the current directory. Copy it to your server, and from the server run this command:

npm install --no-registry -g shiny-server-0.2.2.tgz

Let me know if you have any other problems.

> > > No no, it was great. We were wondering whether circular dependencies worked or not. It turns out it works fine on the released version of Shiny, but did not on our upcoming version--so damshiny helped us find and fix a pretty gnarly bug!
> > >
> > > So, thank you!
> > >
> > >
> > > On Wed, Jan 16, 2013 at 1:54 AM, Vincent <mostly.ha...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > Wow. Sorry to cause so much trouble :) The latest commits had a similar idea of separating the regression and the button handling code. I'll change this to use an observer.
> > > >
> > > > Thanks Joe!
> > > >
> > > > On Tuesday, January 15, 2013 4:43:43 PM UTC-8, Joe Cheng [RStudio] wrote:
> > > > > Hi Vincent,
> > > > >
> > > > > I spent most of today looking at your code, it turned out to be extremely interesting because there is a circular dependency in there. main.regression both reads and writes the dataset.
> > > > >
> > > > > I made a fix that puts the button-handling code in a much more sensible place, and sent you a pull request, BUT it looks like I was using a version of your code that was two commits back. I couldn't understand the last two commits with a quick look and don't have more time today to look at it. But I wanted to explain to you what is different about my commit, so you can figure out the right thing to do to your current code.
> > > > >
> > > > > The core issue was that main.regression contained the button-handling code. That means it is handling two completely distinct tasks: calculating the regression, and responding to the button clicks. These are not only two distinct tasks, but they are also distinct in nature: the former task has no side effects, its return value is depended upon by other reactive stuff, and you can trust the reactive system to let it run whenever; the latter task is all side effect (updating the data), nothing depends on it directly, and it MUST only execute when the button is clicked.
> > > > >
> > > > > To me that means these are screaming to be two separate entities. Calculating the regression is a reactive function, and handling the button click is an observer (using the actionButton/isolate pattern to make sure it only runs on click).
> > > > >
> > > > > Once I extracted the button handling code and put it in its own observer, everything seemed to work.
> > > > >
> > > > >

messages.subject: AJAX in Shiny
messages.subject_clean: AJAX in Shiny
messages.body_plain:
First of all, thank you for the amazing work on Shiny.

I am looking to solve the following -

1) User has 5 plots to rate.
2) As user rates 3 out of those, an AJAX request is sent to do some expensive computation and fetch next 5.
3) When user has rated all 5, the page refreshes with the plots fetched in (2).
4) Repeat (1) and (2) at some interval, say every 5 items.

So this is not reactive. I do not want the plots to refresh as soon as the user rates them.
However as the computation is expensive, so I do not want the user to wait for them at the end of 5 plots (cannot use the submit button solution).

Can server.R be coded in a webservice way that html can call with some arguments (say getNext5(user, plots_rated, ...) ) and get back JSON for this? Are there better solutions?

Thanks

messages.subject: Some changes for next version of Shiny
messages.subject_clean: Some changes for next version of Shiny
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone -

We've made some changes for the next release of Shiny. There are two big changes from Shiny 0.2.4. The first is that reactive functions are now lazily evaluated. (Note that this is distinct from R's lazy evaluation.) What this means for you, as a developer, is that reactive functions will be evaluated more efficiently. You may have noticed that sometimes reactive functions are run multiple times, even when they really only need to be run once. The switch to lazy evaluation should reduce the number of times that reactive functions are run, resulting in a more efficient use of resources.

The other major change is that we've added something called a reactive values object. You can use a reactive values object for storing intermediate values -- ones that take a value from `input` and which will be used for `output`. This is especially useful if calculating the intermediate value takes a lot of time, and is used by multiple reactive outputs: you can calculate a reactive value once, and then use it in multiple reactive outputs.

For any of of you who have already used the reactiveValue() function that was in development, please note that there's a major change in how it's used. This is the old way, which no longer works:
  # Create the value
  valueA <- reactiveValue(10)
  # Read the value
  value(valueA)
  # Write to the value
  value(valueA) <- 20

The new syntax should feel much more natural for R users. The new way is to create an object which is similar to `input`, and then access its members, like this:
  # Create the reactive values object
  values <- reactiveValues()
  values$A <- 10
  # Another option: create the object with an initialized value
  values <- reactiveValues(A=10)
  # Read the value
  values$A
  # Write to the value
  values$A <- 20

If you want to use these features, install the development version of Shiny on your local machine and give us feedback. We'll release the new version of Shiny to CRAN soon, and once we do, we'll update Glimmer to use it.

To install the latest development version, run the following:
    install.packages('devtools')
    library(devtools)
    install_github('shiny', 'rstudio')

Then restart R.

Enjoy!
-Winston

messages.subject: Shiny Server 0.3.0 released (breaking changes!)
messages.subject_clean: Shiny Server 0.3.0 released (breaking changes!)
messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,

I just published shiny-server 0.3.0 which has two important new behaviors, one of which is a breaking change:
You should no longer append ".shiny" to your application directories. This mechanism was confusing and unhelpful. Now Shiny Server just looks for a file named server.R in a folder to see if it's an application folder.
A new directive directory_index was added and it's enabled in the default config (but not enabled if you have a custom config file--you'll need to declare it yourself if you want it). This means if you have a folder that isn't part of an application and doesn't contain an index.html file, then browsing to that URL will list the contents of the folder.
If you want to upgrade, just running "npm install -g shiny-server" should do it.

-joe

Hm, this is interesting. It looks like the problem is happening because your ggplot call uses jitter. In your plot.compareMeans function, you're doing something similar to this:
  print(ggplot(dat, aes_string(x=xvar, y=yvar)) +
    geom_boxplot() + geom_jitter())

If you take out the geom_jitter(), it no longer keeps running the same plot over and over again.

You can even replace the plot with this, and it'll keep running repeatedly:
  print(qplot(1:3, runif(3)))

In both cases, if you make it deterministic by putting set.seed(44) just before the ggplot, it runs only once. I'll look into this.

-Winston

messages.body_plain:
If you want to create an app on glimmer (via the RStudio server interface), create them in ~/ShinyApps/<appname>, where ~ is your home directory and <appname> is whatever you want. Then you can view your app at:
  http://glimmer.rstudio.com/<username>/<appname>
where <username> is your username.

For example, this is an app on my account on glimmer:
  http://glimmer.rstudio.com/winston/stocks/

The runExample() function is for use in an R session on your local computer. Same goes for runApp(). These functions will run a simple webserver on your computer on port 8100, and then open a browser pointing to localhost:8100.

One approach you could use is to do development on your local computer, and then once your app is functional, upload it to Glimmer.

-Winston

Hi Winston & Joe,

Many thanks for your replies. I found the example from Winston particularly helpful. I had been through the tutorial for reactiveUI before and not quite been able to transfer it to what I wanted.

Below is the code for my corrected toy example. Now on to implementing something useful !

Best wishes,
Andy

#ui.r

library(shiny)

# Define UI
shinyUI(pageWithSidebar(

  # Application title
  h5("to test populating UI selectInput from server result, Andy South, 17/01/2013"),

  # Sidebar with controls
  sidebarPanel(

    sliderInput("numSpSelected", "Top X species",
                min = 1, max = 6, value = 2, step= 1)

    ,uiOutput("choose_dataset")

  ), # end of sidebarPanel

  ## MAIN PANEL ##
  mainPanel(
    h4("full species list :")
    ,textOutput("caption")

    ,h4("chosen species :")
    ,textOutput("speciesChosenText")

  ) # end of mainPanel

)) #end of ui.R

#server.r

library(shiny)

dFSpecies <- data.frame(Name=c("ginkgo","rowan","oak","ash","beech","maple"))

# Define server logic
shinyServer(function(input, output) {

  # Drop-down selection box for species
  output$choose_dataset <- reactiveUI(function() {

    selectInput("speciesChosen", "Choose a species", choices=getSelectedSpecies())
    })

  # to provide a list of selected species based on input parameter
  getSelectedSpecies <- function() {

    as.character( dFSpecies$Name[c(1:input$numSpSelected)] )
  } # end of getSelectedSpecies

  # return the full list
  output$caption <- reactiveText(function() {

    as.character(dFSpecies$Name)
  })

  # return the one selected species
  output$speciesChosenText <- reactiveText(function() {

    as.character( input$speciesChosen )

  })

}) # end of shinyServer()
#end of server.R

messages.subject_clean: Some changes for next version of Shiny
messages.body_plain:
Hi Vincent -

One of the reasons that it was getting confused is because of this line:
    plotOutput("plots", height = 1200)

plotOutput() expected height to be a string that gets passed directly through to the web page. The issue is that the web page expects this string to have "px" at the end, like "1200px".

Because the height wasn't properly set, the web browser uses "height: auto". This was part of a reload loop: as the image loads, the browser thinks the image has almost no height (20 pixels in my browser); and then once the image is loaded, it thinks the image is 600 pixels high, as specified in output$plots. Each time the height changes, the web browser requests a new image from the server, and it just keeps looping.

In the development version of Shiny, we've made it accept a number like height=1200, or a string with "px" like height="1200px", so your existing code should run.

Another thing: in your code you use as.list(input), which is a heavyweight operation. When you call that from a reactive function, that function now depends on every single object in input. So if any input object changes, that reactive function will be invalidated and will need to re-execute. Because this is a large dependency, I would suggest not using as.list(input), and instead accessing just the objects that you need from input.

We know that as.list() is a natural idiom to use for R programmers, and in the future we're going to make some changes to make it more clear when you want to take a dependency on all input objects.

-Winston

> > The problem is that R is single threaded so while the long execution is happening, the entire server is blocked. I was trying to think of a way of using fork or some distributed processing R package to get it to execute asynchronously but I'm afraid I'm not familiar enough with those aspects of R to tell you.

To start off I am relatively new at using R, but I have been trying my best to learn and soak up knowledge as much as possible.

A little background:
My job recently tasked me with coding a user interface to show clients data we have collected for them on a website. I stumbled upon this package and in a limited time was able to produce tables that were live queried from our mySQL! AWESOME!

My next task is to add in more intractability with respect to date, charts ect.

 I made a simple drop down bar that lists device names in which each device queries the SQL data base and up pops the data associated with that device.

selectInput("sweetsense", "Device:",

WORKING CODE
datasetInput <-reactive(function()(sqlQuery(ch,paste("SELECT * From ",input$sweetsense,"_Events",sep=""))));

CODE W/ ERROR
datasetInput <- reactive(function()(sqlQuery(ch,paste("SELECT FROM_UNIXTIME((PeaksP1Time),'%Y %D %M %h:%i:%s %x'), PeaksP1, FROM_UNIXTIME((PeaksP2Time),'%Y %D %M %h:%i:%s %x'),PeaksP2 FROM ",input$sweetsense,"_Events",sep=""))));

Error:
Error in UseMethod("xtable") :
  no applicable method for 'xtable' applied to an object of class "character"

I hope I have given enough detail, if not I answer any and all questions. Any help would be most appreciated.

Zak White

>

> I've noticed that if I change my SQL query with respect to how dates are printed I get an "x table" error
